description: Gruvbo is an old mining settlement grown into a small town among forested ridges and lakes, where iron ore has been dug since the Middle Ages. The mine is worked in shares by the mining farmers (bergsmän) and, increasingly, by a Stockholm company buying them out. Smoke from charcoal stacks and the blast furnace at the works stains the sky, and the little ore railway carries ore down to the landing on the lake, where canal barges take it on towards Lake Mälaren.
seasonNotes: October. Charcoal burners are building their stacks in the forest for the winter's hauling, and the blue smoke of the kilns hangs in every valley. Rain and fog roll in off the lakes; the spoil heaps run with rust-red water. It is dark by six, and the shift change at the mine happens by lantern. The first ice skins the puddles at dawn. Farmers are bringing in turnips and potatoes between shifts.
travel: From Uppsala by post-coach (sleigh in winter) west to Sala, about nine hours; sleep there, then by road to Gruvbo, about five hours. In the open season one can also go by rail to Stockholm, Mälaren steamer to Västerås, the Strömsholm Canal to Ängelsberg landing and the ore railway up. A day and a half in all.

authorities.police: The kronolänsman of the Gruvbo district sits in Sala, most of a day away by road; a parish constable and the mine's own watchmen keep order in the town between his visits.
authorities.court: Häradsrätt for the Bergslagen mining district at Sala, with sessions a few times a year (the dates are approximate). Ore-claim, wage and mine-accident cases come here.
authorities.doctor: The provinsialläkare for the Sala/Bergslagen district lives in Sala and drives out to Gruvbo when sent for or to sign death certificates. Between times people go to the apothecary or the wise woman.
authorities.post: Post office at Gruvbo Station; the mail comes by the road from Sala twice a week, and by the ore railway from the landing in the open season.
authorities.telegraph: State telegraph office in the station at Gruvbo, wired through Sala to the national network. It is closed at night and on Sundays except for urgent messages.
authorities.bank: Nearest bank is the savings bank in Sala (30 km); the Westmanlands Enskilda Bank in Västerås (80 km) finances the works and the Stockholm company.
authorities.newspaper: Westmanlands Läns Tidning, Västerås, comes with the post two or three times a week; the reading society also takes the Stockholm papers.

journey.journeyScene: The post-road west runs through spruce and birch, then thickens into forest ridges where the farms thin out and the first charcoal stacks smoke blue. At Sala the inn is full of mining talk and the smell of tallow, and in the morning the hired carriage climbs into the hills past lakes and smouldering stacks. Near Gruvbo the road crosses the ore railway, where a little engine drags its wagons down towards the lake. Then the forest opens on the town, with its furnace glow and the black headframe above the old workings, and the smell of sulphur in the cold air.

publicFacts: The Storgruvan mine has been worked for at least five hundred years; its oldest galleries are said to be dug by fire-setting alone.
A Stockholm mining company has bought up more than half of the old bergsmän shares in the last ten years, and many shareholders resent it.
The ore railway has run from the mines down to Ängelsberg landing for twenty years; canal barges take the ore on to the Mälaren, and in winter it piles up at the landing until the ice breaks.
The mine pumps were flooded in the spring of 1871 and three men drowned; the company installed a steam pump afterwards.
The Gruvbo reading society keeps a library above the apothecary and takes the Stockholm papers.
Hired miners from Värmland and Finland live in the company barracks and drink at the inn on paydays.
The parish has a temperance society, founded by the vicar's wife, which few miners have joined.
A wise woman lives in a cottage out by the tarn, and miners' wives go to her for burns and coughs.

places.name: Storgruvan
places.ownerRole: the mine foreman (gruvfogde), who answers to the shareholders and the Stockholm company
places.description: The great pit opens in the hillside like a wound, its walls stepped and rust-streaked, dropping into fog. A horse-whim creaks in its timber house as a pair of horses walk endless circles, winding up the ore buckets. Water drips everywhere and the clang of hammers on drills echoes up from below. The air smells of wet rock, powder smoke and the steam pump's coal.

places.description: The church is a big plain building of plastered stone, enlarged twice for the mining population, with a squat tower. The air smells of wet wool and candle smoke.

monthVariants.seasonNotes: January. The lakes are frozen hard and the winter roads run across the ice, staked with spruce boughs. Daylight lasts from nine to three; the shift change at the mine is in darkness both ways. Charcoal and ore go by sledge now, and the carters work every hour the frost allows. Snow lies to the windowsills, and the spoil heaps are white humps with rust bleeding through.
monthVariants.travel: From Uppsala by sleigh west to Sala along the post road, most of a day if the snow is packed, then by sleigh into the hills to Gruvbo; a day and a half in all, two if it snows.
publicFacts: In winter the ore railway is often closed by drifts for a day or two, and the canal is frozen, so the ore waits at the landing until spring.

placeDescriptions.mine: The great pit is rimmed with ice and its stepped walls hang with frozen waterfalls. Steam from the pump house rises straight up in the still cold, and the horse-whim's horses wear sacking against the frost. Lanterns move far below in the dark.
placeDescriptions.farm: The old bergsman's homestead stands deep in snow on the lakeshore, a path shovelled from the door to the byre. Smoke rises from every chimney. The lake beyond is a white plain, crossed by the staked winter road.
placeDescriptions.inn: The Ore Wagon is crowded and steaming: carters warming themselves between loads, their sledges and horses packed into the yard under blankets. The windows are thick with frost flowers.
